1:
Everything in the chapter turns on a preposition, and the witnesses split evenly over it. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) sets out the problem squarely: the Hebrew can mean that David's heart yearned for Absalom or that it was set against him, the versions take the first, but the particle is commoner in the second sense and unquestionably hostile at the one other place the phrase occurs in this form (Dan. 11:28) — so he renders it against Absalom, and observes that otherwise Joab's stratagem would have been unnecessary. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) read it the same way, noting that David had not repealed the banishment even after he was comforted for Amnon. Against them, Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) takes the warmer sense: the heat of David's displeasure was over, his old affection survived, and he wanted only a friend to court him to a reconciliation that would not impeach his justice. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) agrees and explains the paralysis — the king desired to see his son but was ashamed to show kindness to one whom the law and his own conscience obliged him to punish, and wanted a fair pretence, which Joab supplied.

On Joab's reasons the witnesses are complementary rather than opposed. Henry counts four: the courtier anticipating what his prince already wanted; the friend who had a kindness for Absalom, or at least looked on him as the rising sun; the statesman who knew how much Absalom was the people's darling and feared civil war if David died while his son was in exile; and the delinquent, conscious of Abner's blood and aware that mercy shown to Absalom would help secure his own reprieve. Keil and Delitzsch allow the personal attachment but make the calculation primary — Absalom had the best prospect of the throne, and Joab judged this the surest way to escape punishment for his own murder — and they add the verdict the chapter withholds: the issue frustrated every one of those hopes — Absalom never succeeded, Joab did not escape, and David was severely chastised for his weakness.

The instrument is chosen with care. John Gill (reformed) observes that the scene was deliberately laid at a distance so that the matter could not easily be inquired into, and canvasses where Tekoah was — Kimchi putting it in Asher, others in Benjamin, Gill himself in Judah, and Jerome giving twelve miles from Jerusalem in one place and nine in another. Ellicott fixes it five miles south of Bethlehem on a high hill, and draws a point from the geography that the others miss: Bethlehem was Joab's own town, near enough for him to have had personal knowledge of this wise woman. He also defends her, finding no ground for the suspicion that she was a witch or disreputable, and notes that the parable was Joab's contrivance yet still demanded skill from her. Both mention that Tekoah was Amos's home, Gill adding that some supposed the woman his grandmother.

Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) accounts for the success by enumerating what was built into the disguise. She was a widow, so her condition of life was calculated to excite compassion. She lived far enough off that the case could not readily be checked. She was advanced in years, which Josephus thought gave her application more weight. She put on mourning to heighten the impression of distress. Her story was framed to run parallel to David's own, to convince him that sparing Absalom was reasonable. And — the point Ellicott makes independently — the likeness was deliberately not drawn too plainly, lest the king see the intention before he had granted the pardon. Henry adds that a mourning widow was certain of a hearing from a king who had himself written that God is the judge of the widows (Ps. 68:5).
4:
Whether any of the tale is true divides them. John Gill (reformed) calls it flatly a fable, and says she pressed for sentence because it would not bear an inquisition. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) treats it as Joab's contrivance. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) alone allows that the principal facts may have been real, Joab having found a woman whose circumstances already resembled what he wished represented. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) take no view of its truth but work on its grammar, explaining the doubled object in the clause about the brother's death from the diffuseness of ordinary conversation, and refusing the emendation some propose since the plural would be quite unsuitable. Ellicott notices what the invention is careful to do: she presents the killing as unpremeditated and without malice, which makes her case essentially unlike Absalom's — but the object here is to dispose the king favourably, and by the time the application comes that distinction will have passed out of mind.

Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) sets out the motive she imputes to the kinsmen: they demand the survivor not out of affection for justice or for the dead brother's memory, but because by destroying the heir the inheritance falls to them — which, he notes, they impudently avow. Gill marks that not the avenger of blood alone but the whole kindred rose as one man. Clarke works the metaphor of the quenched coal, a man and his descendants being often called a lamp in Scripture — as when David's men swore he should go out to battle no more, lest the light of Israel be quenched — so that to quench the coal is to destroy all hope of posterity. Ellicott adds that she puts the threat against the heir into the family's mouth because that would be the effect of what they ask, a covert allusion to Absalom as David's heir being certainly intended.

The king then yields four times over, and Henry counts the steps. First he will consider and give orders — not let the law take its course, though she has gained nothing firm. Clarke observes why that would not serve: too distant to conclude her business, so she pressed on. Her next move is to offer herself as surety, and the witnesses divide on what she is doing. Clarke and Ellicott read it as assuming the blame for condoning blood-guilt, lest the king think his justice compromised; John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads it the other way about, as a warning that neglect of her cause would bring guilt on the king himself, phrased so decently as not to seem to threaten him — and argues that this sense agrees best with the answer David gives. Henry's caution is that her willingness to bear the blame would not acquit a judge who sentenced without due cognizance of the case.

The third concession is protection from molestation, which Henry makes a principle: magistrates ought to be the patrons of oppressed widows. The fourth is the pardon itself, and the request to remember the Lord is read three ways: Gill and Ellicott as adjuring an oath, since to make mention of God is what men do when they swear; Wesley as invoking God as witness against the king should he break a promise already made; Clarke as an argument from the divine example, that God gives mercy promptly and does not wait until the case is hopeless, so that delay here would be fatal. Henry hears a plea to consider how gracious God is, who spared Cain and forgave David the blood of Uriah. The oath follows that not one hair shall fall; and Henry, doubting whether David did well to shield a man the cities of refuge would not have sheltered, allows that as the case was put there was room for mercy to rejoice against judgment.
12:
The mask comes off, and the first difficulty is whom she means by the people of God. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) says that by constant usage the phrase can only be Israel, and that her point is that the king wrongs the nation by leaving Absalom — whom she never names — in exile, against the spirit of the ruling he has just given. John Gill (reformed) prefers the same sense but reports another from Abarbinel, that Ephodaeus understood the phrase of Absalom and his men, or of Absalom alone, one man being sometimes called a people. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) reject a third reading, that of Dathe and Thenius, who understood the phrase of the protection the king had extended to her own son; the construction, they say, will not bear it. All agree the wording is deliberately indefinite, hinting rather than saying.

The argument from mortality divides them more sharply, and over its worth rather than its sense. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) calls the verse very elegant and powerfully persuasive, and partly adopts it: Amnon's crime was the most flagitious, the injury to Absalom in his sister's ruin indescribably great, the king had not administered justice, and so the fratricide, horrible as it is, is pardonable. Gill judges the reasoning plausible but bad in the case of a malefactor, though he grants her insinuation its force — that David must die, that a successor must be named, and that a disputed succession could be fatal if Absalom were not recalled in his father's lifetime. Ellicott thinks she craftily withdraws attention from the real point, the question of right and justice, and assumes what ought to be proved before urging that delay is unsafe because life is uncertain. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) spells out the three deaths in view, the king's, Absalom's, and Amnon's had he not been cut off.

Inside that verse lies a textual crux, and here Clarke and Ellicott agree against the English. Both say the Hebrew is not that God respects no person but that God does not take away the soul; Ellicott renders the whole, that God takes not away the soul but devises thoughts that he may not banish the banished one, and finds the sense to be that God in wrath remembers mercy and will not press punishment to extremes. Clarke adds what the versions made of it: the Greek gives that God will receive the soul — which he takes to show its translators, and the Jews of their time, already held the soul's separate existence after death — and the Latin that God does not will the soul's destruction. Wesley alone works with the received English, reading it of no man being exempted from the common law of dying.

Then the king sees through her. Ellicott admits he cannot say why David fixed on Joab, guessing either a courtier's natural interest in the heir or, more likely, that Joab had pressed the same request before; Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) supplies the reason Ellicott lacks, that no such woman would have appealed to him in a matter of that moment of her own accord, and the king knew nobody so likely to have set her on as a man at once politic and Absalom's friend. Keil and Delitzsch judge her speech so crafty that David could not fail to see both her meaning and that she had not come unprompted, and read her closing flattery as a bid to gain him over completely. Henry's interest is that she did not keep the credit for herself: finding the scheme had pleased the king, she still told the truth about whose it was, and he makes her an example that nothing can ever need a lie. Clarke hears in the compliment about an angel's wisdom the ordinary style of eastern flattery.
21:
The order is given in a form the witnesses find worth weighing. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes that the Hebrew text has the king say I have done this thing while the margin reads thou hast done: the first is simply how a request is granted, the second would carry an implied censure of Joab's stratagem even while complying with it. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) likewise keep the written text here and treat the marginal reading as a misunderstanding. John Gill (reformed) places Joab close at hand, waiting on the issue of the affair, and Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) supposes he had been present throughout the audience, with others of the court besides.

Joab's thanks then settle a question the chapter leaves open. He blesses the king and says that today he knows he has found grace, in that the king has fulfilled the request of his servant — and Keil and Delitzsch draw the inference that he had applied for Absalom's return repeatedly before, without any attention being paid, which is precisely why David had guessed whose hand was behind the woman. That is the reason Ellicott had said could not be known, offered as a guess and here supplied from the text itself. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) hears something further in the gratitude: some have taken it as Joab's assurance to himself that the murder of Abner would now never be called to account — in which, Henry observes, he was mistaken, as the charge laid on Solomon would show (1 Kings 2:5-6).

On the recall itself Henry and John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) are severe in the same terms. Henry cannot see how David is to be justified in suspending the ancient law that whoso sheds man's blood by man shall his blood be shed (Gen. 9:6), and says God's laws were never meant to be cobwebs that catch the little flies while the great ones break through; Wesley puts it that the king had no power to dispense with God's laws, which bind rulers as much as the people. Both reach the same verdict on what followed — that God justly made the son whom a foolish pity had spared into a scourge to his father. Henry alone turns the recall the other way as well, reading in the orders an image of the divine method, since God is reconciled to sinners not immediately but through a Mediator who intercedes and is told to go and bring them again.

The half-measure that follows splits them three to two. Clarke judges it highly proper, a way of showing detestation of the crime and respect for justice while remitting the death penalty. Wesley agrees, both lest the king seem to approve the sin and because the exclusion might draw Absalom to a more thorough repentance. Henry gives two reasons of the same colour: David's own honour, that he might not appear to countenance so great a criminal or to forgive too easily, and Absalom's greater humiliation, since something in his conduct when Joab fetched him suggested he was not truly penitent. Against all three, Keil and Delitzsch call the half forgiveness an imprudent measure that bore very bitter fruit, and Ellicott separates the two acts by their motives — the return granted in weakness, the exclusion out of a sense of justice — and judges the compound effect unfortunate, since it irritated Absalom while leaving him conveniently placed to lay his plots. Ellicott thinks it likely he was confined to his own house. Gill adds only that the king gave the order to Joab when told Absalom had reached Jerusalem.
25:
The beauty is noticed for its political effect, and on that they agree. John Gill (reformed) says it is recorded to account for his hold on the people's affections, then and afterwards; Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) puts it more bluntly, that his person was what made the public interest itself in him, the mass of men being caught by outward appearances; John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) makes it at once the occasion of his pride and of their affection. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) read the hair as part of the same impression, a strong growth being taken for a sign of manly vigour. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) will allow the fact and nothing more: it is a poor commendation for a man with nothing else valuable in him, and though his body had no blemish his mind had nothing but wounds and bruises. He cautions that the hair is not a Nazarite's — Absalom being far from that strictness — but a beau's, worn long because pride feels neither cold nor heat; and he notes what it came to (2 Sam. 18:9).

The two hundred shekels divide them five ways. Keil and Delitzsch call the figure a round number and much too high, since even were the royal shekel half the sacred one the total would stay excessive, the sacred reckoning giving six pounds. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) reaches the same arithmetic and concludes that a clerical error crept in during copying. Clarke agrees the text is corrupt but alone says where: the letter standing for two hundred could easily be read for the one standing for thirty, whose upper stroke is often worn in manuscripts, and takes thirty to be the original — adding that the phrase rendered at every year's end means rather at convenient times, and that the head was polled, not shaved. He preserves two rival solutions while rejecting both: Bochart's defence of the received figure from the lavish ancient use of oil and ointments, with Josephus on the Jews putting gold dust in their hair that it might flame in the sun; and the view that the word gives the value, not the weight. Henry holds the first of those, reckoning the weight lower and citing bishop Patrick that with the oil and powder the figure is not incredible; Wesley records the second without deciding. Josephus's own reckoning, which Clarke reports and derides, runs to twelve and a half pounds and a head that took eight days to shear.

On the children they converge. Gill, Keil and Delitzsch, Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley all infer from the omission of the sons' names that they died young, and point to the pillar Absalom raised for want of a son to keep his name in remembrance (2 Sam. 18:18). Henry allows that but offers another, that the sons may have been cut off by God while he was hatching his rebellion, the monument following their loss. Keil and Delitzsch take the daughter's name for evidence of Absalom's affection for the sister Amnon had violated; Ellicott adds that she shared her namesake's beauty.

Her later history is the sharpest dispute. Clarke reports that the Greek adds she became Rehoboam's wife and bore him Abia, that Josephus agrees, and that no other version has it. Keil and Delitzsch answer that it is at variance with the record that Rehoboam's wife and Abijah's mother was Maachah, and that Thenius defended it as original on grounds Böttcher showed to be worthless. Ellicott calls it a confused gloss but is alone in rescuing its substance: Maachah is called the daughter of Absalom, yet Abijah is elsewhere called the son of Michaiah the daughter of Uriel, so Maachah must be Absalom's granddaughter — Tamar married Uriel, and it was her daughter who became the mother of a line of kings.
28:
Two more years pass in the city without a sight of the king, and the witnesses disagree about where the fault lies. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) hold to their verdict that the half forgiveness was worse than none at all, and read the whole episode as its fruit. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) puts the blame the other way: after three years abroad and two as a prisoner at large Absalom had been dealt with better than he deserved, yet his spirit was unhumbled and his pride unmortified, and instead of being thankful that his life was spared he reckoned himself wronged not to be restored to his place at court. Had he truly repented, Henry argues, the distance from the gaieties of the court and the retirement of his own house in the holy city would have suited him well — if a murderer must live, let him be for ever a recluse. John Gill (reformed) states the grievance plainly, that he was uneasy at being confined to his house and not suffered to come to court. Henry sees through the longing to see the king's face: it was pretended love and real ambition, and the snake could not sting again until it was warmed in its father's bosom.

Why Joab would not come is answered two ways. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) supposes he judged he had gone far enough already, that he was himself still under the king's displeasure, and that he may have thought Absalom should show some sign of penitence for so great a crime. Henry finds a smaller and more personal motive — that Absalom had never thanked him properly for the recall, proud men taking every service done them for a debt — and observes what a man in Absalom's position would ordinarily have done, which is to send a civil message and a handsome present. Keil and Delitzsch note only that the summons went twice and was twice refused.

The barley field is where the chapter shows what Absalom is. Keil and Delitzsch explain the calculation exactly: the field adjoined his own and stood full of grain, and he foresaw that Joab would not take the loss of his property quietly but would come to complain of it. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) calls the conduct strange and notes the irony that it worked — Joab, who had not used his influence to get Absalom to court, now uses it and succeeds. Ellicott grants the stratagem was perfectly successful and adds the judgment the success invites, that it would only have been resorted to by a lawless and unscrupulous character. Henry reaches for a comparison and finds that Samson could think of no greater injury to do the Philistines, and marvels that a man should expect to win a kindness by doing a mischief. Gill observes drily that Joab came provoked, and to learn the reason — which was exactly Absalom's end.

Henry alone notices what the law required and nobody asked. Absalom was bound to make restitution for the burnt corn (Exod. 22:6), yet there is no sign that he offered it or that Joab demanded it; Henry's explanation is that Joab may have thought he could not justify his own refusal to come, so that each man let the other's fault pass. He also suspects fear in it — that Joab, alarmed at such boldness and reckoning that Absalom must already have an interest among the people strong enough to carry him through, not only swallowed the injury but went on the errand, which shows what some men can accomplish by threats and carrying things with a high hand. Against that Henry sets the one comfortable reading of the fire: that God by afflictions brings to himself those who keep at a distance from him.
32:
Absalom's answer offers his own life, and what to make of that offer divides the witnesses four ways. John Gill (reformed) sees no repentance in it at all: he neither denies the deed nor is ashamed of it nor asks pardon, but sets about vindicating it with a reason he thinks sufficient. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) reads it as something bolder than vindication — a message haughty and imperious, unbecoming either a son or a subject, which undervalues the favour already shown in the recall from Geshur, denies the crime outright, and then defies the king's justice in words the speaker knows are safe, since he counts on being loved too well for them to be taken up. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) grants that no wrong is acknowledged, yet gives the demand a logic the others withhold: the half-reconciliation is intolerable, and the man must either be punished or fully pardoned. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) go a step further and allow that Absalom might very properly desire to be dealt with according to the law. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) hears only flattery — better to die than to want the sight and favour of a dear father — and takes it for a calculated insinuation into the affections he means to exploit.

Wesley also marks the trajectory. By this time, having so far recovered his father's favour, Absalom had begun to grow upon him, and had gathered confidence enough to stand on his own justification, as though what he had done were no iniquity, or at least none deserving death. Gill notes only that Joab carried the message as it was given him.

On the kiss they are of one mind about the king and divided about what it teaches. Ellicott judges plainly that David showed great weakness here, and suffered severely for it afterwards. Henry agrees and locates the error precisely: the king's strong affection construed the posture and the words as the language of a great respect and an earnest desire of his favour, when it was far otherwise, and the lesson is how easily wise and good men are imposed upon by children they are blindly fond of. Wesley puts the same warning in almost the same words. Keil and Delitzsch, who called the earlier half-measure worse than no forgiveness at all, let the full reconciliation stand as its inevitable sequel.

Yet both Henry and Wesley refuse to end on the politics. Absalom bowed himself to the ground and the king sealed the pardon with a kiss; and from that they turn the scene round on the reader. If the bowels of a father prevailed to reconcile him to a son who had not repented, they ask, shall penitent sinners question the compassion of the Father of mercies? Henry presses it with the prophet's word that when Ephraim bemoans himself God soon bemoans him, calling him a dear son and a pleasant child (Jer. 31:20) — the argument running from the lesser case to the greater, since what mere fondness did badly, mercy does justly.
